articles.title: Is Donald Trump ready to do business with Myanmar?
articles.summary: There are signs the United States is shifting its policy towards Myanmar, formerly a global pariah.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
A top US official recently met with Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing for the first time in years By Jonathan Head South East Asia correspondent 
- Published 58 minutes ago 
Has Washington's long-standing policy of isolating the military regime in Myanmar now changed? 
The revelation that a top official in the Trump administration met its leader Min Aung Hlaing last month, and the removal of some business figures from the US sanctions list, suggests that it has. 
Until now, the US had had very little official contact with the regime following the 2021 coup, when Myanmar's military ousted democratically-elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi. More recently, it had applied a series of targeted sanctions against those judged to be supporting the junta. 
The meeting on 15 and 16 September was with US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance, and it took place in Myanmar's capital Nay Pyi Taw. Its ostensible focus was to secure the release of Adam Castillo, a US citizen who had been detained in June over a dispute with the local American Chamber of Commerce. 
But Vance was the most senior US official to meet Min Aung Hlaing since he seized power, and they almost certainly discussed other matters of mutual interest. 
Vance is also known to have met Burmese officials in Tokyo in June, again in Tokyo this month, and to have met representatives of the groups opposing military rule. 
Signs of a shift in US policy towards Myanmar, though, go back to July last year, at the height of President Donald Trump's tariff war. 
That was when Min Aung Hlaing, along with other leaders in the region, received a personal letter from the US president informing him that his country's shattered economy was about to be hit by, in Myanmar's case, 40% tariffs. 
Other countries reeled in shock at the punitive levies imposed on their vital trade with a country they had once seen as a friend and ally. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Much of Myanmar has been devastated by a civil war that has been raging since 2021 
But Min Aung Hlaing was delighted. 
He replied immediately to express his "sincere appreciation for this encouraging invitation to continue participating in the extraordinary Economy of the United States, the Number One Market in the World", mimicking Trump's hyperbolic phrasing and eccentric capitalisation. 
"It is with great esteem that I wish to acknowledge Your Excellency's strong leadership in guiding your country toward national prosperity with the spirit of a true patriot." 
This was not just a dictator's hunch that flattery might be the best way to win favours from Trump. Min Aung Hlaing's coup, and the civil war it ignited, had turned him into an international pariah. 
His regime was largely unrecognised. He was accused of being a war criminal, with cases lodged against him at the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice. Aside from Russia and, more recently, China, he was shunned by other governments. 
Yet here was the US president addressing him just like any other president or prime minister, as "Your Excellency. There was no mention in Trump's letter of the appalling human cost of Min Aung Hlaing's power seizure; of a democracy crushed and leader Aung San Suu Kyi jailed. 
That same month the regime signed a $3m (£2.3m) contract with DCI, a long-standing Washington lobbying firm which had been used by a previous Burmese military regime in 2002 to try to improve its image. 
Since then the military government has also hired Roger Stone, a controversial lobbyist and confidant of President Trump, at a fee of $50,000 a month. 
Also around the same time Adam Castillo, a former US marine and Trump supporter who had just stepped down as president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Yangon, was in Washington trying to persuade Vice President JD Vance's team that it was time to re-engage. 
Castillo believed that the US reliance on sanctions to isolate the junta had failed. 
"Myanmar mattered to America not only as a morality play but as a strategic interest," he wrote in his book Finding Our Voice: A Story of Leadership in Crisis and the American Spirit Abroad. He discussed with the vice-president's team how the US "could engage Myanmar without war or isolation, loosen China's grip on critical minerals, and align peace with American interests". 
Figure caption, 
Watch: The rebels at the front line of Myanmar's civil war 
Castillo was pushing at an open door. 
The US dependence on rare earths from China had been exposed when China blocked them in retaliation against Trump's tariffs in April. The administration began prioritising finding alternative sources. Myanmar happens to have large reserves of rare earths which are currently being exploited solely for China's use. 
At almost exactly the same time, the state department issued new guidance to US embassies around the world on what to say about elections. From now on, it said, "messages should avoid opining on the fairness or integrity of an electoral process, its legitimacy, or the democratic values of the country in question". 
So, when Myanmar held its much-criticised general election in December and January, allowing Min Aung Hlaing to turn himself from coup leader into a notionally civilian president, the US did not, like most Western governments, condemn it as neither free nor fair. 
For decades the US has consistently pronounced judgement on other countries' elections. Now the US had nothing to say. 
Washington's decision to lift sanctions on some of those targeted by the Biden administration seemed only to confirm the new direction of US-Myanmar policy. 
"For years, the US approach to Myanmar has been defined by isolation, sanctions, and distance," wrote the lobbyists DCI in a recent newsletter. "That era is over… thankfully, President Trump has the courage to try something different." 
The tone is certainly different, but not so much the substance of US-Myanmar relations. 
"In practice less has changed than the headlines suggest," says Richard Horsey, Myanmar adviser for the International Crisis Group, adding that Min Aung Hlaing is still sanctioned. "What is new is the level of contact and the location. Senior US officials have now been to Nay Pyi Taw, which is exactly what Min Aung Hlaing wanted. What he wants next is sanctions relief, and that will be harder." 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Myanmar's leader Min Aung Hlaing on a recent diplomatic visit to Malaysia 
It was another Trump initiative last year, though, which has arguably had a much greater impact on Myanmar: the dismantling of USAID, which slashed aid to opposition groups, dissident media and refugees by more than half. 
There was also the decision, decried by human rights groups, to withdraw Temporary Protected Status from 4,000 Burmese who had sought sanctuary in the US. This has left them living in fear of being sent back, where many face being jailed, or worse. 
As for the rare earths in Myanmar, few experts believe they will ever be of much use to the US. Most lie in areas contested by ethnic insurgent armies. 
They are currently extracted by Chinese companies with long experience of operating in these lawless borderlands, and transported over the border to China for processing. It is difficult to see how the US could get access to them. 
It is also doubtful that the US will get meaningful co-operation from the Myanmar government in combating the scam industry. 
There have been a few highly-publicised actions against some of the larger scam compounds, but the syndicates running them have simply dispersed to smaller operations in more remote areas, and in any case most are run with the support of militia groups allied to the Myanmar military. 
"Talking to Nay Pyi Taw is not wrong in itself," says Hunter Marston, Southeast Asia director at the Lowy Institute. 
"The question is what Washington asks for and what it gives away. It should use the channel for the things that matter most: humanitarian access, an end to airstrikes on civilians. It should keep talking to the opposition and the ethnic armed groups, who hold much of the country. And on scams, the most effective thing the US can do is to co-ordinate with other governments in the region, including China, to go after the money." 
Perhaps the bigger question, though, is whether President Trump, distracted by domestic politics and the war on Iran, has the capacity to give any sustained attention to Myanmar, let alone enough to challenge the dominant influence of China.

articles.title: North Korea publishes photos of Kim Jong Un - why do rumours of his death keep coming back?
articles.summary: North Korean state media has published photos of the dictator with his daughter after the unsubstantiated rumour spread.
articles.full_text:
Image source, KCNA Image caption, 
North Korean state media released photos of Kim Jong Un shortly after rumours of his death started spreading online By Laura Bicker China correspondent 
- Published 20 October 2026 
Kim Jong Un has appeared in North Korean state media looking remarkably healthy for a man rumoured to have died from a brain haemorrhage. 
Photographs published by state newspaper Rodong Sinmun show the 42-year-old dictator touring what the paper said was a clothing and footwear exhibition with his daughter. 
The images emerged hours after a Chinese dissident who lives in the US claimed, without evidence, that Kim had been taken to a hospital in Beijing in a coma and had died. 
For those who watch North Korea closely, this kind of rumour has become almost routine. 
In one of the world's most secretive states, facts are often difficult to verify, creating fertile ground for speculation. 
This latest claim originated with Wanjun Xie, who identifies himself as chairman of the Chinese Democratic Party, a group banned by Chinese authorities. He has previously circulated unverified claims, including speculation about the death of Chinese leader Xi Jinping. 
Xie alleged that Kim suffered a severe brain haemorrhage and was transferred to Beijing because North Korea lacked the medical facilities to treat him. 
He claimed Kim later died and that his body had been secretly returned to North Korea, with the regime concealing his death. 
Yet the photographs tell a different story. 
Kim is seen examining displays, accompanied by Kim Ju Ae and his usual entourage of officials. 
While there is no way to know exactly when the images were taken, there are other reasons to doubt the claim. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: What do a teenager's clothes tell us about North Korea's future? 
There would probably be signs beyond North Korea's borders if there were a sudden collapse in Kim's health. 
China could tighten security along its frontier to prepare for potential instability or refugee flows. Activity around North Korean diplomatic missions might also increase. Defectors in South Korea often receive information through informal networks along the Chinese border. None of this has happened. 
South Korean intelligence officials, meanwhile, told Yonhap they had heard nothing to support the reports. 
The rumour also echoes previous false alarms. 
In 2020, a high-profile North Korean defector claimed he was "99% certain" Kim had died following cardiovascular surgery. Not long afterwards, Kim appeared in public and the claim unravelled. 
So why do these rumours keep resurfacing? The first reason is succession. 
North Korea has been ruled by the Kim family for three generations, but what happens after Kim Jong Un remains less certain than it was for his predecessors. 
Kim Il Sung spent decades preparing his son, Kim Jong Il, for power. By the time Kim Il Sung died in 1994, the succession plan was firmly established. Kim Jong Il's transition was relatively smooth. 
Kim Jong Un's rise was faster and more precarious. After Kim Jong Il suffered a stroke in 2008, his youngest son was rapidly promoted through the ranks. By the time his father died in 2011, he had been publicly identified as the future leader. 
Even so, Kim Jong Un spent years consolidating power, purging rivals and eliminating perceived threats. 
Today, South Korea's intelligence agency believes he may be preparing his daughter as a successor. She has increasingly appeared at high-profile events and military displays. 
But she is thought to be only 13 years old. North Korea has never been led by a woman, and she has not been formally designated as heir. Her youth would also leave her vulnerable in any power struggle. 
All of this uncertainty helps explain why rumours about Kim's health attract so much attention. 
Image source, KCNA Image caption, 
South Korean intelligence believes Kim may be preparing his daughter as a successor 
The second reason is that the rumours are not entirely implausible. 
Kim is overweight and a heavy smoker. South Korea's National Intelligence Service has repeatedly warned that his lifestyle puts him at higher risk of cardiovascular disease. Heart problems and strokes also run in the Kim family. 
If anything were to happen to Kim, the stakes are high for neighbouring countries and the wider international community. Any sudden leadership crisis raises difficult questions about control of North Korea's nuclear weapons and the prospect of political instability. 
Would a power struggle tempt hardliners to act aggressively? Could unrest trigger a refugee crisis along the Chinese border? These are questions that concern not only Beijing and Seoul but also Washington, which maintains around 28,000 troops in South Korea. 
Intelligence agencies watch Kim Jong Un closely so they are prepared for any news. 
Because North Korea remains an information black hole, it is also an easy target for false reports. Only a tiny circle has regular access to its leader. Even intelligence agencies struggle to obtain reliable information, and much of what emerges is heavily caveated as unverified or highly likely rather than confirmed fact. 
The regime itself is also suspected of deliberately encouraging confusion, leaking misleading information to obscure what is really happening inside the country. 
So it is hard to believe that Wanjun Xie had somehow stumbled across such significant news, when it had eluded those whose job it is to stay across it. 
He may simply have been seeking attention. Or he may have wanted to embarrass Beijing by highlighting its ties to Pyongyang, although those are well-established for the world to see. 
Whatever his motive, Xie is far from the first person to exploit the uncertainty surrounding North Korea's leadership.

articles.title: A thousand slogans echoed here - but it could be the end for iconic Delhi protest site
articles.summary: Jantar Mantar, an 18th Century site almost synonymous with demonstrations in Delhi, has been denotified as a protest site.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
The "cockroach" demonstrations over the summer of 2026 could well become the last time Jantar Mantar was home to a sustained protest movement By Sharanya Hrishikesh BBC News, Delhi 
- Published 17 October 2026 
What is the point of a protest? 
To raise your voice against injustice? To draw attention to a cause? Or to make those in power uncomfortable enough to listen? 
For more than three decades, Indians have tried to do all three in a narrow, tree-lined road near Jantar Mantar, an 18th Century astronomical obervatory in Delhi. 
But that may now be coming to an end. 
This week, Delhi Police said Jantar Mantar, located close to parliament, would no longer be a designated protest site. 
The decision comes months after the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - not a political party but a collective which began as a joke - led a massive protest there demanding the resignation of federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Tens of thousands turned up and Pradhan subsequently resigned. 
Police barricaded Jantar Mantar soon afterwards, preventing further demonstrations. Last week, an attempt by CJP supporters to march there, this time demanding the resignation of India's election chief, ended in a police crackdown . 
Protesters have now been directed to three other sites. Two are far from parliament, while the third, the sprawling Ramlila Ground, is often booked months in advance. Unlike Jantar Mantar, which is free, all three charge tens of thousands of rupees a day. 
Delhi Police says , external it acted after the Supreme Court suggested identifying alternative sites with adequate infrastructure. But critics say the move could push protests beyond the reach of ordinary Indians, further from the seat of power and into venues many cannot afford. 
Over the years, Jantar Mantar has witnessed everything from mass movements that shook governments to small, lonely demonstrations by people desperate to be heard. Farmers, students, grieving parents and ex-soldiers have gathered under its trees, holding placards and shouting slogans. Not every protest made headlines, but for many, it was a place to turn to when other doors had closed. 
This week, when the BBC visited, those scenes seemed a distant memory. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Jantar Mantar is an 18th Century astronomical observatory in Delhi - the protests were held not in it, but in the road next to it 
Yellow barricades blocked both ends of the road, with hundreds of paramilitary personnel standing guard, batons in hand. 
In a nearby lane, uniformed men sat in shops drinking tea or scrolling through their phones. At one of the few shops without policemen, the shopkeeper folded his hands and said he did not want to answer any questions. 
Built by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II in the 1720s, Jantar Mantar was once better known as a tourist attraction than a place where a thousand revolutions were imagined. 
Its story as a protest site began in 1993, when the then-Congress government stopped allowing demonstrations at the Boat Club lawns opposite the old parliament. 
Historian Harleen Kaur has traced how, from the 1960s onwards, successive governments brought in new rules that shifted the site of protest in Delhi further away from parliament. 
"Jantar Mantar, situated 3km (1.86 miles) from the Parliament House, [allowed the government] to contain protesting crowds at some distance from the Parliament House and PM's residence," she wrote in a 2023 paper , external . 
Yet, the road saw countless spirited protests over the years. 
Rachna Dhingra, an activist with the Bhopal Group for Information and Action, an advocacy group for survivors of a 1984 gas leak disaster, camped at Jantar Mantar with hundreds of others for around five months in 2008, trying to get the government to agree to demands including setting up a commission to allocate resources for rehabilitation schemes. 
Through a scorching summer, they held press conferences, met politicians and even chained themselves to railings opposite then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh's residence to draw attention to their cause. 
It was also where she found solidarity with others - Tibetans protesting against China, activists opposing the displacement of people over large dam projects and even just lone protesters who caught a train from their home towns with nothing but a placard and a grievance. 
"It can be lonely to protest but that place became a home for so many of us. We shared each other's stories, struggles and victories," says Dhingra. 
Image source, Courtesy Rachna Dhingra Image caption, 
In 2008, Rachna Dhingra and other activists camped for months at Jantar Mantar demanding justice for survivors of the deadly 1984 gas leak in Bhopal - when it rained, they sheltered under tarpaulin sheets 
Dipa Sinha, an academic associated with the Right to Food campaign, has seen ground-breaking laws - a landmark rural jobs guarantee scheme , the National Food Safety Act and Forest Rights Act - take shape at Jantar Mantar. 
"It was a place where you could discuss issues with people who came to Delhi from across the country," she says. 
Protesters would demonstrate outside government offices, including the erstwhile Planning Commission and the agriculture ministry, where they were often detained by police, before returning to Jantar Mantar to "gather, discuss and strategise". 
But sustaining a protest for months was not easy. 
Dhingra says they sheltered under tarpaulin sheets when it rained, used public toilets near the site and went to nearby gurdwaras to freshen up. 
In 2017, the National Green Tribunal cited the lack of infrastructure, along with complaints from locals, to have Jantar Mantar shut down for protests. 
A year later, the Supreme Court overturned this, citing the rights to free speech and peaceful assembly guaranteed under the constitution. 
When asked whether the proximity to parliament made a difference to their cause, Dhingra quoted the reactions of her co-protesters who had come to Delhi for the first time. 
"That's the president's house? Does the prime minister live there? How can they not listen to us when we are at their gates?" she remembered them saying. 
Sinha points out that Jantar Mantar was also near institutions like the Press Club and Constitution Club, making it easier to get media coverage, and for politicians to drop by and meet protesters. 
It was a simpler time - sometimes they would ask for permission from police only on the morning of the protest. 
Those rules have become much stricter , external now. 
In recent years, when Dhingra tried to protest at Jantar Mantar, she was told no-one could stay the night. 
"Where do you go with hundreds of people who have travelled all the way to the capital to protest?" she asks. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
In 2006, Narmada Bachao Andolan (Save the Narmada river movement) leader Medha Patkar (grey sari), went on a 20-day hunger strike at Jantar Mantar 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
In 2015, retired soldiers held protests at Jantar Mantar against the delay in the implementation of a pension scheme 
While Jantar Mantar has its supporters, others share memories of an even more vibrant protest culture. 
Mary E John, a gender studies scholar who lived in Delhi both as a student and as an academic, says that before 1993, she attended protests at the Boat Club on issues ranging from workers' rights and women's issues to topics of international significance. 
"We lived in a climate where protest was part of life. In fact, we took it for granted," she says. 
When the spacious Boat Club lawns made way for Jantar Mantar, it actually felt "claustrophobic", she said. 
She pointed out that they, and others before and after them, protested at multiple sites - universities, colleges, streets - instead of just at Jantar Mantar. 
She sees signs of that in protests by farmers who camped at Delhi's borders for months, and people who sat at the Shaheen Bagh neighbourhood demanding the repeal of a controversial citizenship law. 
Even the 2012 anti-rape protests, she points out, were not restricted to Jantar Mantar but almost reached the Indian president's heavily guarded complex and beyond into other parts of Delhi. 
It's not clear what Jantar Mantar's future is - the Supreme Court is hearing pleas challenging its removal as a protest site. 
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and CJP leaders have said that Jantar Mantar belongs to the people and will be "reclaimed". 
As the debate rages on, Jantar Mantar is the quietest it has been in decades - will it hear slogans again?

articles.title: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say
articles.summary: A truck carrying people to a funeral and a market alleged to be supplying fuel to the RSF were targeted.
articles.full_text:
Image source, MSF via Reuters Image caption, 
Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei town has been treating people wounded in Monday's attack on the market By Richard Kagoe ,  Lucy Fleming   and   Richard Irvine-Brown ,  BBC Verify 
- Published 20 October 2026 
Sudan's army has been accused of launching several drone strikes that have reportedly killed more than 300 people, including dozens travelling to a funeral. 
The death toll from strikes in two areas of West Kordofan state on Sunday evening was 150, sources told the Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict that erupted in 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). 
In Abyei, a disputed border area between Sudan and South Sudan, 153 people were killed when drones hit a market on Monday, the region's information minister said. 
A military source told the BBC the army had carried out the Abyei attack, saying the market was a fuel supply site for the RSF. 
The attack has raised tensions between South Sudan and Sudan, which jointly administer Abyei, as they both claim ownership to the oil-rich region in a dispute that has remained unresolved since South Sudan ceded in 2011. 
South Sudan has summoned Sudan's ambassador to lodge a formal protest. There are fears the conflict could spill across the border. 
- 
A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan 
- Published 13 November 2025 
- 
Drones hammer Sudan's gold and oil zone - the pivotal new front line 
- Published 25 February 
Despite a partial arms embargo on Sudan, foreign countries have been supplying both the army and the RSF with drones and they are increasingly becoming the weapon of choice in the conflict. 
The war has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, killed hundreds of thousands of people and forced more than 14 million from their homes. 
"We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting essential services," UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said on Monday , external . 
The rising use of armed drones came as 20 million people faced acute hunger, with a rising risk of famine in parts of the western region of Darfur and Greater Kordofan, he said. 
Greater Kordofan comprises three states and is a vital axis linking Darfur, controlled by the RSF, to the capital, Khartoum, now in army hands. 
The wave of drone attacks started on Sunday evening and, according to the Sudan War Observatory, it is likely they were launched from the army-held city of Kadugli in South Kordofan state. 
A truck carrying around 200 mourners which had travelled from an area north of Abyei was hit as it arrived in the town of Al-Dabab in West Kordofan, the monitoring group said. 
Sources told the group that 145 people were killed and a tent where mourners at the funeral had gathered was also hit, killing five others. A further 150 people were injured in the attacks, it said. 
Army drones also bombed a market in the town of Al-Mujlad in West Kordofan on the same evening, according to the Sudan War Observatory, which said the exact number of deaths and injuries were not yet known. 
Sudan's army has not responded to the allegation it carried out these strikes, but said it did not attack civilians even if they believed there were RSF fighters amongst them. 
The attack in Abyei, which borders West Kordofan, took place on Monday around 11:30 local time (09:30 GMT) targeting Amiet Market around 10km (six miles) from Abyei town, the region's Information Minister Yohana Akol Ngor told Radio Tamazuj, which broadcasts from the Netherlands to audiences on the Sudan-South Sudan border. 
On Tuesday, the minister confirmed to the Associated Press and Reuters that the death toll had risen from 73 to 153 people. 
"It is a horrible and shocking situation," AP quotes him as saying. 
BBC Verify has studied satellite images that show extensive burnt buildings in the north-east corner of Amiet Market, which is also known in Arabic as Al-Na'am Market. Older images from the area show it is usually full of trucks. 
It has also verified footage filmed near the market that shows a large plume of smoke, at least one petrol tanker and someone talking about five missiles being fired. Another verified video shows two massive, separate fires coming from buildings near that section of the market. 
"The market was completely destroyed. The bombing spread terror and fear among the local population," market trader Fadlallah Adam Hamouda told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily. 
Another trader told the BBC the attack had come as shock as UN peacekeepers have been in Abyei since 2011 - with more than 2,800 uniformed personnel currently deployed. 
"Our area is a weapons-free zone under United Nations protection, yet it was targeted by drones," he said. 
"The attack caused extensive material damage after the fuel market was struck, sparking a massive fire that spread to nearby homes." 
Image source, TikTok screengrab Image caption, 
This screengrab is from a video taken 600m from Amiet Market 
Earlier, Ngor told Reuters that emergency workers had struggled to retrieve the bodies because of fires caused by the strikes. 
On Monday, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said it had also received people wounded in the attack at Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei town. 
"So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted. We are providing surgical services and wound dressing, along with other emergency care," MSF's Christian Lindauer, the charity's manager at the hospital, said in a statement. 
Meanwhile, a drone strike near the airport in Khartoum on Monday has killed four people, including three children, the AFP news agency reports, quoting a medical source. 
It also cited a military source as saying air defences in the Sudanese capital had downed several other drones launched by the RSF towards the airport. 
Fighting in Kordofan, a strategic area rich in gold and oil, has intensified over the last year after the army regained control of Khartoum from the RSF.

articles.title: Mission blasts off for Mars to grab a piece of its moon
articles.summary: A spacecraft is set to launch on an ambitious mission to bring 10g of Martian moon dust back to Earth.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Spacecraft heading to Mars' moon Phobos lifts off from Japan By Rebecca Morelle ,  Alison Francis   and   Kevin Church ,  BBC News Science 
- Published 19 October 2026 
A spacecraft has launched from Japan headed for Mars' moon Phobos, where it will attempt to grab some moondust and bring it back to Earth. 
If it is successful, this will become the first time a sample has been returned from Mars or its moons to be analysed in laboratories here on Earth. 
The spacecraft is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in August 2027. 
It is hoped that the Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) mission, which is led by the Japanese Space Agency, will solve the mystery of how Mars's moons formed. 
Prof Sara Russell, from the Natural History Museum, who is the MMX mission's deputy for sample analysis, said: "There hasn't yet been a successful mission to go to Phobos and bring a bit back to Earth. 
"I think this is an incredibly ambitious and fun mission," she said. 
There are only three moons in the inner Solar System: our own Moon, and two around Mars, which are called Phobos and Deimos. 
Both of these are tiny - Phobos is about 20km (12 miles) across and Deimos is about 10km (six miles) across. They are also irregularly shaped, looking a bit like space potatoes. 
The MMX spacecraft will study Deimos as it arrives in the Mars neighbourhood, and then will focus on Phobos. 
It plans to set down a small rover to explore the terrain, though this will be no easy feat. 
Sara Russell says no one has ever landed a rover on such a small moon. 
"The moon itself doesn't have very much of its own gravity," she explained. 
"But it's next to an enormous planet that's got a much higher gravity, and that makes it much harder to get a rover onto the surface." 
Image source, NASA Image caption, 
Mars got its moons about 4.5bn years ago - but no one knows how they formed 
The rover will scout out a landing site so that the MMX spacecraft itself can later touch down on Phobos. 
Once on the surface, it will deploy a robotic arm and two samplers to grab some moon dust. 
This material will be packed into a small capsule that will return to Earth in 2031, landing in the Woomera desert of South Australia. 
The amount of material that will come back is tiny - just 10g. 
"It's a very small [amount] actually," said Dr Chrysa Avdellidou, from Leicester University, who is working with the Japanese mission. 
"However we can do several studies even on individual grains… You don't need to have kilos back from a surface in order to do science. So it's worth every gram," she said. 
Image source, JAXA Image caption, 
The spacecraft will collect 10g of moon dust from the surface of Phobos 
Scientists believe the sample will finally shed light on the puzzle of where Mars's moons came from. 
There are two competing ideas. 
Either a space rock smashed into Mars early in its history, and Phobos and Deimos were created from the debris. 
Or the moons are two wandering asteroids from the outer Solar System, which were grabbed by the Red Planet's gravity. 
"When we get the sample back, we'll be able to look in detail at its chemistry and its mineral composition - and the two hypotheses will produce very distinct results," said Sara Russell. 
"It should be pretty much immediately obvious.. whether it's the product of this dramatic impact or whether it's a captured asteroid. So we'll find that out really quickly." 
The team is also hoping there might be an extra bonus coming back to their labs. 
"One of the really exciting things is that Phobos is so close to the Mars surface that whenever there's an impact into the Mars surface, little grains might actually become implanted into Phobos itself," said Russell. 
"And that means that the sample we get back may actually contain grains of Mars as well. So it can give us really direct information about the composition and history of Mars." 
Image source, Kevin Church/BBC News Image caption, 
Martian meteorites are rare - this one is on display at the Natural History Museum 
Bringing material from Mars back to Earth has long been an ambition of space scientists. 
The Nasa Perseverance rover, which has been exploring Mars since 2021, has been carefully collecting samples on Mars and storing them in canisters. 
But a second Nasa/ESA mission, called Mars Sample Return, that would have picked up and returned these canisters, has been effectively cancelled, after its funding was halted by the US Congress. 
China is planning its own sampling mission to Mars, set to launch in 2028. It will attempt to return Martian material to Earth in 2031. 
We do already have some fragments of the Red Planet here on Earth in the form of Martian meteorites. 
These are pieces of Mars that were blasted off the surface by asteroid strikes, and ended up being hurled towards the Earth. 
Martian meteorites are extremely rare, but like all space rocks that fall to our planet, they become contaminated as soon as they get here, mixing with the air, dust, soil and water. 
Scientists are so desperate to get their gloved hands on a direct sample from Mars and its moons because it would be pristine.

articles.title: Why Israeli Gen Z voters are drawn to the far right
articles.summary: More than half a million young people will cast their ballots in Israel next week - and they could make all the difference.
articles.full_text:
Image caption, 
Far-right minister Ben Gvir (left) has significant support among Israeli youth By Lucy Williamson Middle East correspondent ,  Reporting from Jerusalem 
- Published 20 October 2026 
When Israel's far-right National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, reached voting age, he was rejected from Israel's army for being too politically extreme. 
His views have not changed much in the 30 years since then - but Israel has. Once shunned by the political establishment, he is now part of the government's inner sanctum of ministers. 
On the campaign trail ahead of Israel's general elections next week, Ben Gvir is often surrounded by a jubilant pack of fresh-faced young fans, waving huge party flags over the heads of his numerous security guards. 
At the covered market in Ramle - a mixed city of Jewish and Arab Israelis - he told us his message to young voters was to get out and vote. 
"We see the support, we see the love [and] we want to win!" he said. 
Image caption, 
Nadav, 18, believes Ben Gvir is "trying to show that Israel is a strong country" 
More than half a million first-time voters will cast their ballots in this election, which many Israelis see as existential for Israel's future security and identity. 
Polls suggest it will be a tight race, and the new young voters could help decide the result. 
More than 16% are planning to support far-right parties - either Ben Gvir's Jewish Power or the Religious Zionism party of his far-right ally Bezalel Smotrich - according to a poll for one of Israel's most popular newspapers, Yedioth Ahronoth. 
And almost three-quarters see themselves as "right or centre-right", according to another survey for Israel's leading Channel 12 television network. 
"Itamar Ben Gvir gives me a sense of security," said 20-year-old Mordechai, one of the young fans accompanying the politician to Ramle. 
"Like everyone in history, from Trump to Moses, there are slips of the tongue that are a bit less good. So what? 90% of the things by Itamar are amazing." 
"Itamar will give us safety, and when we go to the army, someone will have our backs and be behind us," said 18-year-old Nadav. 
"I think he's trying to show that we're a strong country. For many years, we couldn't show we're strong in our beliefs. We couldn't express our ideology." 
Meir Schreiber, an ultra-Orthodox 23-year-old who grew up in London, said the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel, which triggered the Gaza war, also convinced him that Ben Gvir was the right choice. 
"Young people understand that peace isn't something we can do," he told me, "because what happens to you when you're young shapes your personality - we saw October 7." 
Image caption, 
Polls suggest more than 16% of first-time voters are planning to support far-right parties next week 
Ben Gvir is a divisive candidate in a divided nation: his political positions include annexation of the occupied West Bank, Jewish settlement of Gaza, and the "voluntary emigration" of Palestinians - positions and rhetoric that are widely condemned by liberal Israelis. 
Several Western countries have imposed sanctions or travel bans on Ben Gvir and Smotrich for incitement against Palestinians. Both men are powerful ministers in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's governing coalition. 
As he and his entourage pushed their way between the stalls, some shopkeepers threw sweets; others, dark looks. 
"I don't like him, he sows discord," one stallholder said. "Ramle is a mixed city - Jews and Arabs. There's no problem here, even after 7 October, but his message preys on young uneducated people." 
The fact that he appears more popular with 18 to 22-year-olds than with their parents' generation is often put down, at least partly, to the impact of the 7 October attacks. 
But political analyst Dahlia Scheindlin, who previously ran many Israeli political campaigns, said it was more than that. 
"For about the last 20 years, we've seen young Israeli Jews are more right wing than average, and significantly more right-wing on many measures than the 55+ group," she told me. 
"They have grown up under a series of wars with no personal experience of efforts to achieve peace. But for the most part, they have been socialised into the most extreme terms of the debate [as] legitimate to discuss: annexation, settlement expansion and - after 7 October - annexation of Gaza. And now they're voting for the first time." 
Image caption, 
Mordechai, 20, says Ben Gvir's "slips of the tongue" do not matter 
A series of classroom debates filmed by Israeli satirist Lior Schleien recently highlighted the extreme views of some young Israelis. 
The debates, in which he challenges racist or extreme views, drew a lot of attention in Israel, and included one exchange in which a student advocates killing all Arab citizens of Israel. That particular video has since been removed from Schleien's website. 
Surveys suggest that first-time voters here are highly motivated to cast their ballots, with more than 80% saying they are likely to do so. But the same research suggests they are also more sceptical about democratic institutions and less engaged by political protests or petitions. 
In a race that is largely deadlocked between two stable blocs of pro-government and anti-government supporters, getting new voters to the polling stations could make all the difference. 
Opposition parties have been engaging younger voters with warnings about threats to democracy, new social media videos and younger candidates. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Polls show Benjamin Netanyahu and his coalition allies in a tight race with the opposition bloc 
"In 2022 [in the last election], only 59% of the citizens living in Tel Aviv voted - in the most liberal city in the whole Middle East! In places where they voted for Ben Gvir, they voted at around 90%," said Yonatan Shalev, a 24-year-old candidate with the centre-right opposition party, Beyachad ("Together"), led by former prime minister Naftali Bennett. 
He told me that Ben Gvir had understood the power of social media faster than other politicians. 
"The liberal politicians didn't believe in TikTok, didn't believe in Instagram, and he took advantage of that arena." 
Shalev said he had pushed his own party to reach young voters through social media. 
"Three months ago, Ben Gvir was still the politician with the most amount of views on TikToks, the most amount of likes on TikTok, and Instagram as well," he explained. "Right now, Naftali Bennett is leading [that]." 
His boss's Instagram page now features videos of the former prime minister lifting weights to rap music, or chatting with Shalev in the street. Even Netanyahu has joined in with a fast-paced militaristic social media video set to heavy beats. 
"Younger people don't watch the news in Israel, [they] don't read the newspapers. The younger generation is getting all its details from TikTok and Instagram". 
Image caption, 
Beyachad candidate Yonatan Shalev says Ben Gvir understood social media's power sooner than others 
Yahlee Reske and Mika Magal, both 21 years old, rushed out of a nearby bar when they saw Shalev walk past. 
"I love him," Mika told me. 
"Yes," agreed Yahlee. "He's our age, he's so young and knows so much. It's hard to listen to people who are old and saying the same things over and over again." 
Yahlee said she was doing national military service when the 7 October attacks unfolded. 
"I don't think I ever looked at politics until then," she said. "But maybe if the government had been different on 7 October, things would have been better." 
The same poll suggesting 16% of first-time voters would back a far-right party also suggested that Beyachad alone would take almost 9% of their votes, as would the centre-right Yashar party of Gadi Eisenkot. 
At a student event in Tel Aviv last weekend, Ben Gvir was interrupted by protesters shouting, "Fascism will not pass", and forced off the stage. 
Israel's young voters may be moving to the right, but they are still as divided as their country, over who they believe is the guardian of Israel's security and identity, and who is an existential threat.

US bans use of China’s DeepSeek AI tools by government agencies
Use of tools ‘may result in the transfer of sensitive data’ to China, defense department says 
The US government on Monday ordered its agencies to stop using artificial intelligence (AI) tools from the Chinese startup DeepSeek , as the countries race for dominance in the fast-moving sector. 
A notice from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced the ban on products developed by DeepSeek – and tools created using DeepSeek by third parties – saying they must be removed from IT devices. 
The DHS can issue direction to civilian agencies but not the military or intelligence services. The US defense department did not respond to an AFP request for comment. 
“DeepSeek’s models present multiple threat vectors,” said a document attached to Monday’s notice. 
Use of DeepSeek AI tools “may result in the transfer of sensitive data to [China] if used by US government employees or vendors”, the department warned. 
Its servers are located in China, where the legal system permits the government “extensive authority” to access private company infrastructure, it said. 
DeepSeek has been contacted for comment. 
One of China’s top AI labs, DeepSeek shook up the industry in January 2025 with a low-cost, high-performance chatbot, challenging assumptions of US dominance. 
The firm released a long-awaited new model, V4, in April, and earlier in October updated a faster, more lightweight version of V4. 
The US has accused DeepSeek and other top Chinese AI firms of systematically stealing the capabilities of cutting-edge models developed by American rivals. 
Despite their fierce competition in the field, when their leaders Xi Jinping and Donald Trump met at the White House in September, China and the US agreed to set up a “communication channel” for AI incidents. 
The topic is expected to arise again at a meeting between Xi and Trump at a summit scheduled for November in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

Russia wants America and China to decide Ukraine’s future without Kyiv. Europe must challenge this dangerous return to diplomacy of the strong for the strong 
D oes Vladimir Putin know exactly how to play Donald Trump? The history of chummy phone calls, high-profile meetings and attempts to bring Russia in from the cold certainly suggests that Moscow’s thuggish ruler has a hold on this American president. If Mr Trump agrees to negotiate Ukraine’s future with Mr Putin and China’s Xi Jinping without Ukraine at the table, he will have handed the Russian leader a victory before talks begin. The message will be that strongmen are ruling the world and determining the fate of weaker nations. 
Ukraine has the right to determine its future. That right cannot be waved away by a self-serving Russian proposal, however much it indulges Mr Trump’s belief that world affairs should be settled by powerful men. The scales are falling from European eyes. Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments. If Washington now rewards Moscow and pressures Ukraine to accept a raw deal, it would be a betrayal . European governments would wonder where America might be in the future when their own security is threatened. 
View image in fullscreen 
Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping. Photograph: China Pool/Getty 
The Wall Street Journal laid out how Mr Putin is hoping to secure a diplomatic prize that dwarfs any US benefits. Mr Trump needs to bring down diesel prices before crucial midterm elections. So the Russian president has offered him a deal that helps the White House claim it is addressing such costs, despite most analysts saying that it won’t. In the same conversation, Mr Putin suggested a summit to end the war in Ukraine that would elevate Moscow and exclude Kyiv. China could also gain recognition as a diplomatic mediator, while Europe would be left out of discussions about ending a war on its continent. Reports suggest that the three leaders could meet at next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China. 
American presidential power is meant to be constrained by law and democratic institutions. Mr Trump’s diesel deal appears to violate US law barring imports of Russian ‌energy until Moscow ends its aggression against Ukraine. More Republicans should find the courage to stand up to their bullying president. While doing so, they might also ask why the order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine ​for battlefield communications and drone operations reportedly came from the White House . Heated denials from the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio , are no substitute for answers. 
A transatlantic breakdown in relations between European powers and the US is not inevitable. Mr Trump’s national security strategy last year called Europe “ strategically and culturally vital ”. But it also demanded that the continent take responsibility for its own defence. European governments must prepare to meet that challenge. 
History doesn’t repeat itself, but it often rhymes. Were Mr Trump to embrace Mr Putin’s trilateral summit, it would echo the Three Emperors’ League that brought together Germany, Austria-Hungary and Russia in 1873. Germany sought to isolate defeated France and contain Austro-Russian rivalry, while monarchies sought to defend themselves against revolution. The original arrangement quickly unravelled. Revived in 1881 , the league collapsed in 1887 as Vienna and Moscow failed to reconcile their Balkan ambitions. Agreement between powerful rulers provides no guarantee of a lasting settlement. Ukraine’s future cannot hang on bargains struck to stroke the egos of powerful men.

View image in fullscreen

China’s economy grows faster than forecast after AI boom boosts exports
Third-quarter GDP up by 4.5% compared with last year as industrial output is buoyed by electronics demand 
Roaring exports lifted China’s economic growth in the third quarter of this year, with factory output growing much faster than consumer spending. 
China’s GDP grew by 4.5% year-on-year between July and September, the National Bureau of Statistics of China reported on Monday. The figures were better than economists had expected and up from the second quarter’s growth rate of 4.3%. 
China’s economy has now grown by 4.6% in the first nine months of the year, putting it on track to hit the government’s 2026 target of 4.5%-5% growth without extra stimulus measures. 
Industrial production rose 5.5% in September, up from 5.2% in August, while retail sales only increased 1.1%, up from 0.4%. 
Duncan Wrigley, the chief China economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said Beijing’s policymakers were likely to conclude that their efforts to stabilise headline growth in the third quarter were successful. 
“Headline industrial production rose in September partly as coalmines resumed operations after safety inspections prompted by a major accident. Manufacturing output growth remained robust at 6.0% year on year in September, buoyed up by stronger export demand for electronics, AI-related equipment and autos,” Wrigley said. 
“Hi-tech manufacturing output continues to outperform traditional sectors, as China climbs the value-added ladder,” Wrigley added. 
However, fixed-asset investment fell 7.2% over the first nine months, property investment tumbled by 20.6%, and infrastructure spending remained weak. 
Data last week showed that China’s exports surged by more than a third in September, lifted by a rise in shipments of electronics related to AI. 
“This pickup in GDP growth mainly reflects ongoing export strength on the global AI/tech boom, more than offsetting drags from the Iran conflict and ongoing weakness in domestic demand,” said analysts at ABN Amro.

In the three weeks since a health worker’s death in Siberia, officials have stonewalled the WHO – setting a worrying precedent for future pandemics 
I s there a plague outbreak in Russia? If the answer were a clear yes, there shouldn’t be much reason to worry. With swift medical intervention, plague is treatable. But in the nearly three weeks since a worker at a Siberian plague research unit died of a mysterious respiratory illness, state officials have been consistently tight-lipped about what happened and whether there were any further cases. 
It is this uncertainty that has the World Health Organization (WHO) and international community worried: partly because there is a – very small – risk of an outbreak, and partly because it is yet another warning that the international coordination we rely on to prevent pandemics is fraying along with the rest of international politics, and could easily fail to protect us in the future. 
The key to containing an outbreak is quick disclosure and open sharing of information. Russia reportedly held high-level meetings about the case, quarantined the hospital where the worker was treated and traced about 200 contacts. That response suggests officials believed the infection was plague, and yet they did not report any of this to the WHO, as international law requires. Russia later revealed that the worker died of a pneumonia of unknown origin – hardly useful information. It undoubtedly gathered lab results and genetic sequences that could shed more light on the case, but has not shared them. 
View image in fullscreen 
The logo of the World Health Organization. Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty 
Earlier this year, the hantavirus outbreak originating on the MV Hondius cruise ship was successfully contained , showing that the global health system can still work well when countries cooperate. This latest incident suggests that one recalcitrant nation can jeopardise everyone’s safety. It is not the WHO’s fault that Russia is essentially a rogue state, but the body must be ready for such eventualities. International politics is fragmented, and only becoming more so. 
Earlier this year the US left the WHO (though it is still party to some of its treaties). States follow international laws when they believe in them, or when they believe that there will be penalties – reputational or otherwise – for not playing along. The WHO has not attempted to play hardball with Russia, or set off a round of international condemnation from leading member states. Some might be heartened that on 7 October the US state department officially requested that the Russian government share information with the WHO. However, it is likely that this reflects Washington’s increasingly ad hoc approach to international politics – using every lever available as situations arise – rather than a renewed commitment to international law. President Trump said on the same day that he would speak to Vladimir Putin about the issue. If that happened, no one has heard about it or what information may have been revealed. 
The keen US interest may give credence to speculation that what in fact happened was some kind of bioweapons research leak. This is thought to be unlikely, but not impossible. The fact that such a scenario can even be plausibly entertained three weeks after the initial event speaks to a serious breakdown in the system. Western states probably do not hold much sway with Russia . But the other Brics nations may have more. The WHO used to rely on US backing for its requests. It may now have to find support among wider, more multipolar coalitions. This potential outbreak may come to nothing, but there will be another soon.

Why Britain should reject the lure of cheap – and scary – Chinese AI
Phillip Inman 
-

In the west the technology comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent – not so from China 
There is much to fear from artificial intelligence developed in China and handed to businesses and governments in the west almost free of charge. 
Every month Chinese AI developers such as DeepSeek and Xiaomi dispatch the latest versions of their “open-weight” models that allow users to take the core software and use it without paying an expensive ongoing licence. 
In Britain, we love cheap Chinese kit, usually setting aside any concerns about how it was made and who by. 
The row over whether to allow Chinese electric cars unfettered access to British retail forecourts is a case in point. They are cheaper than other EVs sold in the UK and, consumers ask: What is not to like? These same consumers might consider how Chinese EVs are subsidised by Beijing deliberately to boost exports and, in so doing, undermine foreign domestic car industries. 
Cheap AI takes this export threat to a higher level. 
It’s scary because Beijing is entering a new phase in the long march of economic development, taking the world’s second largest economy closer to making China great again. 
Go back 10 years and Xi Jinping’s close supporters were alert to the internal contradictions of a totalitarian, command and control state apparatus and how it could trigger social unrest, much as it did in the last century in Tiananmen Square . 
A property crash that still acts as a drag on the economy, rising unemployment, poor health services in many regions, a mismatch of men and women, an ageing population – they could all be the spark that threatens Communist party rule. 
Then came AI and the state discovered complete control. 
Now Beijing has huge surveillance capabilities, using AI to capture images of its citizens and monitor their activities if they need to. 
Don’t think it means Chinese people are under virtual house arrest. They can go about their daily lives, gathering in the street for an impromptu dance or to discuss how their local region might be better run. But serious dissidents? They are rooted out and sidelined, re-educated or punished. 
For the central committee, AI is a blessing. While the financial constraints from having to please a domestic audience have not entirely disappeared, Beijing’s leaders can concentrate on the threats they face from the rest of the world. 
Not that it wants to invade countries in the same manner as Russia. China’s reinvigorated belt and road initiative creates permanent channels for trade less obviously than the previous iteration, allowing Beijing to turn states into clients who depend for the basics of life on Chinese technology. 
Where Russia is using AI to enhance cyber-attacks on European government agencies and businesses to create chaos, China wants merely to widen the circle of friends that consume its goods without asking awkward questions. 
Military force is also being contemplated. Now that Beijing can redirect precious resources previously needed to subsidise Chinese consumers, it is building a fleet of warships to challenge the US in the Pacific, much as Japan did in the 1930s. Taiwan, the engine of semiconductor development, is in its sights. 
Meanwhile, Chinese developers are launching AI models by the dozen each month at a fraction of the cost of US equivalents. 
There are tech analysts who say Chinese models add to the rich tapestry of AI, supplementing the closed, proprietary models of OpenAI and Anthropic. And they say there are European and Indian versions in development. Adding to that tapestry, Meta is fast developing open AI models, but like the other challengers, lags in the race to win over customers. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion 
In practice, an AI user has the choice between a cheap Chinese open system they can tweak for their own ends or expensive US software that comes with bells and whistles they probably don’t need. 
Both types have the potential to destroy humanity, as many AI experts have documented . But on a more mundane level, in day-to-day use, only one comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent, and it’s not the Chinese option. 
As Ross Burley says, Chinese AI comes with extra baggage. Burley is director of the Centre for Information Resilience (CIR), an independent, non-profit group dedicated to, among other things, exposing human rights abuses and countering disinformation. 
He says DeepSeek cannot access the properly isolated use of its software, “but that addresses just part of the risk. Running a model on your own servers doesn’t automatically remove any political censorship. Or indeed repair weaknesses in any security defences.” 
An evaluation report by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (Nist) found political censorship in downloaded DeepSeek models running on its own infrastructure, which means that hosting those models in the UK wouldn’t, by itself, remove censorship. 
“We should be deeply concerned about embedding Beijing’s political restrictions into systems that businesses and public services rely on for information and decisions,” he says. 
The policy governing DeepSeek’s online chatbot says it collects prompts and uploaded material, processes and stores personal data in China, and permits disclosure to Chinese authorities. 
Michael Wooldridge, a professor of AI at the University of Oxford, says it is not unreasonable to assume data inputted into the chatbot could be shared with the Chinese state . 
The consequences for policymaking are profound. The UK should reject the lure of cheap Chinese AI and seek to better tame US AI while supporting domestic and EU suppliers. 
Relying on Chinese tech, from cars to AI, is going to hollow out industry and undermine the security of our data.
